policies.summary: After June 30, 2025, a county, city or other local authority may prohibit the siting, construction, permitting or deployment of electric generation projects by developers other than Indiana retail utilities, their affiliates and electric cooperatives or joint agencies for no more than one year, and may not extend or renew the prohibition.

Counties and municipalities decide siting of wind and solar through local zoning; there is no state siting permit. State default standards apply only in communities that volunteer to become wind or solar energy ready communities (see IN-state_setback_standard-1 and -2).

In a county or municipality that voluntarily adopts the state wind standards, turbines must be set back 3 times tip height from nonparticipating homes, 1.1 times from nonparticipating property lines, roads and airport runways, 1 mile from state parks and municipal boundaries (waivable by the municipality), and meet a 50 dBA hourly sound limit at homes; local height limits may be no stricter than FAA rules.

In a county or municipality that voluntarily adopts the state solar standards, commercial solar must be set back 250 feet from nonparticipating homes (or less with a landscape buffer), 50 feet from nonparticipating property lines and 10 to 40 feet from roads, panels may be no taller than 25 feet at full tilt, and sound may not exceed a 50 dBA hourly average at neighboring homes.

restrictions.description: Resident opposition to possible commercial solar projects and need to review zoning rules for commercial solar, battery storage, and data centers. Active. Legal basis: Board of Commissioners action on Plan Commission recommendation, effective 2026-02-25; ordinance or resolution number not captured in publicly accessible Dearborn County records (CivicClerk portal renders client-side) as of 2026-04-29.

Council sought time to develop city standards addressing electrical grid capacity, water and air impacts, sound, and setbacks before accepting new hyperscale data center and BESS applications. Active as of 2026-09-23. The Elkhart Common Council voted 9-0 at an Aug. 27, 2026 special meeting to pause acceptance of new data center and battery energy storage system applications through Dec. 31, 2027, or until the city adopts development standards, while staff research electrical grid, water, and air impacts. Applies only within the city of Elkhart, not surrounding Elkhart County. Legal basis: Elkhart Common Council ordinance, adopted 9-0 at a special meeting on 2026-08-27, pausing acceptance of new data center and battery energy storage system (BESS) applications.

Concern that a developer could apply before the county had standards for data centers, BESS, and carbon sequestration. Active as of 2026-09-23. An Aug. 13, 2026 Plan Commission workshop on green energy/data center development standards confirmed the moratorium (enacted 2026-02-23 on data centers, battery storage, and carbon sequestration) remained in effect, with Plan Commission Director Kim Hostetler stating there were still no active data center project proposals in the county. County Commissioner Rob Miller said the county "has paused data center development." Continued Plan Commission/public process activity through September 2026 (community meetings, a since-cancelled Sept. 22 Plan Commission meeting) indicates the permanent UDO data-center regulations were still being drafted, with no replacement ordinance located in sources reviewed as of this date. Legal basis: Ordinance No. 2026-04, "An Ordinance for the Adoption of a Text Amendment to the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) for Huntington County to Place a Moratorium on Data Centers, Battery Energy Storage Systems and Carbon Sequestration Projects".

County review of UDO standards after solar project controversy; concern that newer technologies, including data centers, were not adequately addressed. Active. Legal basis: Ordinance No. 2025-11-17-1 establishing a moratorium on new small modular reactors, data centers, solar energy conservation systems, and wind energy systems.

Jay County, Indiana commissioners approved an updated wind farm ordinance on May 11, 2026: setbacks of 1,500 ft from property lines, previously 1.5 times the tower height, which landowners may waive in writing; permit fees raised to $2,500 per MW. They also repealed the one-year moratorium on new wind farm developments, which was to run through July 21.

Jay County, Indiana commissioners approved an updated commercial solar farm ordinance on May 11, 2026, 2-1 (Monroe dissenting): setbacks of 250 ft from property lines, up from 25 ft, which participating and non-participating landowners may waive in writing; permit fees raised to $2,500 per MW and development plan fees to $50,000. They also retroactively repealed the solar moratorium.

Jay County, Indiana commissioners approved a new battery storage ordinance on May 11, 2026, after a public hearing: facilities 500 ft from property lines, equipment inside a 7-ft security fence set back 50 ft, permitted only in agricultural-residential zones by special exception from the Board of Zoning Appeals, $2,500 per MW permit fee. They also repealed the moratorium on battery storage facilities, which had ended April 28.

According to the Allen County zoning ordinance, last updated in September 2019, wind energy conversion systems with any of the following three characteristics are prohibited: (a) a nameplate capacity of more than 50 kW; (b) a total height of more than 60 feet; and (c) a total swept area of more than 40 feet.
In April 2024, the Boone County Board of Commissioners adopted a new 2-year moratorium on large-scale solar, wind, and storage projects.
In November 2024, the Clark County Commission issued new requirements for solar projects.
Clinton County, Indiana, upheld a moratorium on wind farms.

On February 22, 2022, the Delaware County Commissioners approved amendments to the County’s solar ordinance, including increasing the setback from neighboring property lines to 200 feet and classifying solar as a “special use” subject to public hearings and additional approvals.
According to the Fulton County zoning ordinance, last updated in October 2018, wind farms are prohibited in all unincorporated areas of Fulton County.
Under the Unified Development Ordinance of 2022, wind turbines must not exceed 300 feet in height and must be set back by at least 1.5 times the tower height from property lines.
As of April 2019, twelve of the fifteen towns within Henry County had passed resolutions establishing buffer zones where no wind projects could be built.

In 2018, Miami County increased wind turbine setbacks to 2,000 feet from property lines and roadways amidst local opposition to a proposed 75-turbine project in the northern part of the county.

Whitley County requires setbacks from property lines equal to 6.5 times the height of the tower or 2,640 feet, whichever is greater.
The Wells County Zoning Ordinance, last updated in November 2022, prohibits “large” wind energy conversion systems throughout the county.

A 2016 ordinance passed by the Wayne County Commissioners provides that large wind energy systems with a capacity greater than 50 kW or a total height of more than 100 feet are “not a permitted use.” While the ordinance sets out a procedure for small wind energy systems to obtain permission as special exceptions, the ordinance does not appear to provide a similar procedure for large systems.

In 2017, Wabash County tightened its restrictions on wind development, requiring 3,960-foot setbacks from most buildings, zero shadow flicker on the properties of non-participants, and a 32-dBA limit.
An ordinance adopted in September 2021 requires that wind turbines be set back 2 miles from property lines and roads.
In 2016, a few years after the opening of the divisive Wildcat Wind Farm, Tipton County amended its wind ordinance to require setbacks of 2,640 from residences and 1,500 feet from property lines.
In 2019, Tippecanoe County Commissioners voted to prohibit all wind turbines over 140 feet tall in all unincorporated areas of the County.
In May 2023, Spencer County adopted a year-long moratorium on the permitting of commercial solar projects.
In October 2024, St. Joseph County Council increased solar setback requirements.
Rush County limits turbines to 200 feet and imposes a setback distance of 2,640 from all property lines.
In 2018, Pulaski County Commissioners banned all commercial wind development.
In January 2021, the Posey County Commission voted to prohibit all turbines within 10 miles of the Doppler Radar Site in Owensville.
Since 2013, Noble County has required a 3,960-foot setback from property lines for wind projects.

In December 2023, the Madison County Board of Commissioners unanimously approved a solar ordinance that requires solar farms to be set back 3 miles from waterways and other solar farms and that limits solar farms to 400 acres in size.

projects.description: In September 2024, the Madison City Council voted to deny a rezoning proposal that would have allowed the proposed Aypa Power solar farm to proceed in Madison, Indiana.
The Henry County Planning Commission rejected a proposal for the Big Blue Ribbon Wind Farm in 2019 amidst community opposition to the project.
In October 2023, the Clark County Board of Zoning Appeals denied a special exemption permit for a 3,900-acre solar project proposed by developer BrightNight.

In October 2021, Elkhart County commissioners voted against rezoning agricultural land for a 150-MW solar energy project near Millersburg, Indiana.

On March 30, 2023, nine local residents filed a lawsuit to reverse the Howard County Board of Zoning Appeal’s February 28 decision to grant a special exception permit to ENGIE for the proposed Emerald Green Solar Farm.

In May 2015, the Rush County Board of Zoning Appeals included in a special exemption permit for the Flat Rock Wind Project the condition that all turbines be set back 2,300 feet from non-participating properties.
Averon Energy and Tenaska proposed a 280-MW solar project near the City of Princeton in Gibson County as part of a power purchase agreement.
Grandview Solar Project LLC is seeking to develop a 91-MW commercial solar project in Spencer County that would span 37 parcels of land.
In December 2019, the Hamilton County Board of Commissioners rejected plans for a 4-turbine, 11-MW project by Hamilton County Wind.

In September 2018, developer RES Americas canceled plans for a 600-MW wind farm in Indiana several months after Miami County increased its setback requirement to 2,000 feet from property lines, roads, public lands, and city limits.

Plans for a $1.5 billion, 1,300-MW solar project have encountered opposition from a resident group called Pulaski County Against Solar.
Community members have expressed opposition to the Meadow Forge solar project in Delaware County, Indiana, citing concerns over visual impacts and loss of tax revenues for local schools.

Juwi Wind withdrew its proposal to construct a 150-MW wind farm in 2014 in Tipton County after the County’s Zoning Board of Appeals restrictions made it essentially impossible to proceed.

On July 22, 2024, the Bartholomew County Board of Zoning Appeals denied a conditional use permit to the 200-MW Swallowtail Solar Project.
